title: digital silence as practice
content:
from my podcast, botanical studies of internet magic

listen on apple listen on spotify

this is about escaping the noise of platforms and constant connectivity. I reflect on why acclimating to digital silence can feel stark, lonely, and hard, at first. it's like how the body feels on "airplane mode," or when when waking up in a forest after a decade in a cramped city apartment.

in this episode, I explore how and why platforms (by design) turn us into static noise. I share my personal experiments on digital minimalism and solitude -- as a way of practicing more presence and here/now-ness, wherever you are.

this is a meditation on digital silence as a rich landscape, showing you a deeper way into the self.

this week's episode was inspired by a question from a student during office hours of House on the Webs. and she asked me, she's an artist. she said to me, I have maybe one last post on Instagram before I move my energy to my website and my newsletter. and she asked, how do you acclimate between the sudden change in noise levels and stimulation? and I don't think she said this, but the feeling of being alone.

the urban transition metaphor

the best way that I can think to describe this sudden change in stimulation and digital noise is how your body feels, your psyche feels when you move from crowded, dense urban environments, the cities to a secluded place in nature, or even the suburbs. suddenly the lack of stimulation, the lack of constant sirens and neighbors and car noises honking outside feels unsettling, stark, if that's not what you're used to. and then it feels like an exhale.

it feels like your body, your psyche can just let go of constantly being fed some external input or constantly needing to put up defenses against external interruptions.

over time, as you acclimate, or maybe over a day or even a few hours, you start to feel that the silence of nature is not really silence. you tune more deeply into the sounds of the wind, the birds, the rain, the house, the atmosphere. it's not just your sense of sound, it's all of your senses seem to heighten.

and maybe the difference isn't as dramatic as I'm making it sound like. it's not like you become a superhuman with superpowers when you move out of the city. but I think the same thing happens when you consciously remove yourself from the digital noise.

defining digital noise

and social media is a very clear example of spaces with a lot of digital noise, but I think this question of noise versus silence, different forms of silence, applies not just to social media, but also to technology in general, to checking the news, checking my email, to any kind of information.

and of course, it's so relative because what sounds like music to me could be noise to someone else. when my partner is watching sitcom videos on his phone in the other room, to me that's noise interrupting my work, but to him it's a funny enjoyable moment in his day. so maybe what defines noise versus sound or things that we actually want to engage with is how much do we consent?

all information is not noise, but the information that we do on autopilot or because we're trained to do so, where we feel a compulsion, it adds noise to the space of the psyche.

and I want to unpack what is it that's so hard about moving from noisy digital spaces into silence?

I think if you're an artist or creator sharing your work on Instagram or a writer on Substack, you don't think that you're allowing yourself to be consumed by noise until you make a decision that it is noise.

I think first off, there's a shift when you decide that platforms such as Instagram or Substack are manipulating your attention in a way that makes you feel like your life would be better without it.

not the people, but the platforms

so let me be clear about one thing. when you're sharing your work in a community of other artists or writers on Instagram or Substack, it's not that their work is noise for you or for me, it's that the platform itself, the meta structure, the way that it's designed, the way that it manipulates your attention, the way that it dangles carrots of external validation, those things create the noise of the atmosphere.

I think we go to platforms with very real desires to connect, to feel part of a web of other creators, to get inspiration, to give inspiration, to be in a reciprocal flow with others, and also a need to feel contextualized, part of something greater, part of a network, a community of people doing similar things. it can be lonely and isolating to work on your own website or in your own newsletter, and to feel like an island into yourself.

it's so human to want to feel connected, that we're in a space where we can be reachable, where we can reach others, like we can extend our hands and touch someone else, but platforms, by the nature of their design, turns each other into static noise. and I define noise as something that is not given full presence and attention, because attention itself becomes a scarce resource.

so platforms, by diminishing our capacity to pay attention, by making you feel poor in attention through overstimulation, through addiction tactics. what originally was real human connection. slowly over time, you feel that you don't have the resources to be able to engage with it, and you just scroll past it or take a fleeting glance at it and everyone is aware that we don't have infinite attention.

that creates a reinforcing cycle of how we show up on these platforms, how we need to shout louder and louder so that we don't become the noise. the solution to not becoming someone else's noise is to remove yourself from the environment that creates the noise.

digital hypervigilance

but platforms aside, I think that the disorientation and the fear and the emotional challenges that come with reducing the digital noise in our lives definitely speak to underlying fears of, if I'm not keeping tabs on this or that, then something bad could happen.

it's a form of hypervigilance, a need to be connected or to be aware of things that are outside of our physical environment. like I need to keep my phone on in case my parents text me in case something has happened, or I need to keep checking my email again and again in case my client is mad at me or she hates me and I need to know that. this hypervigilance applies to digital life and the ways in which we allow ourselves to be porous in our boundaries between how we engage with the world of information and how we contain ourselves.

my digital solitude experiments in Japan

during the spring of the pandemic, I was in Japan for a couple of months living in the countryside with a friend. it was locked down. I felt very, very far away from all the fast-paced lives that I was living before. and I made a conscious decision for those couple of months that while I was in isolation, living with my friend in the countryside, I was going to experiment with different forms of digital solitude.

I started by deliberately deciding not to be on social media for those months at all and not checking my phone until noon. and then I experimented with other things like, what if I didn't check my phone until 3 p.m.? what if I didn't check it until 5 p.m.? what if I didn't consume any form of news other than what was physically there? what if I went a day without using any screens?

and that was a ritual that I kept. I called it screenless Sundays. and it was amazing to discover what it feels like to engage with the physical world, to be outside, to do things around the house, like I was eight years old again.

what if I kept my phone on airplane mode until 5 p.m. or until the sunset? what if I consumed and responded to all of my messages or emails in a period of one or two hours, as if I was living on a remote island or on a cruise boat or on an airplane? what if airplane mode was the mode of my life? and connectedness was something that I had to plan for and budget for, kind of like being in military service.

my partner went to military service and could only use a flip phone. and we would make plans to talk to each other once a week for an hour or two. and in many senses, it made our communications more deliberate, more present. I would save things to tell him during that one or two hours and write them down. that's what I did in Japan.

instead, I had a lot of time to walk in nature, to collect wildflowers, to make art, to write, come up with games to play, to cook, to really be in the physical world, to be in my body, to be in the place.

and I discovered that the more digital solitude, the more silence that I practiced and deliberately cultivated, the richer my inner world felt. I would wake up bursting with ideas. the days would feel vibrant. or I would fall into cycles of emotional drama and tsunami weather, and that was fine too. at least it was part of my natural ecosystem and not digitally mediated or digitally exacerbated. at least I could live it like a fever and then recover on my own terms.

I think in those months during quarantine and the collective hermitude of the lockdown, the way that I dealt with the anxiety and the uncertainty of the future and where I was going to go, where I was going to be, was to be as present as I could in this moment, in the moment in which I was physically.

and looking back, those were some of the happiest months of my life. mostly because I felt so present and able to savor and enjoy small daily pleasures, like making my bed or cooking a dinner together with my friend or going on walks. it was a total recalibration of my system, a reset of the way in which I relate to life, my sensitivity to my environment and the world around me.

one of the many reasons why I left New York City was that it was so overstimulating that I had to compensate by putting up a numbing shield. and I didn't like what that numbing shield, the wall, did to me. and I think this is the case with our digital lives too. being in certain digital environments can change the way that we relate to others and to ourselves.

part of what made my time in Japan feel so precious and so contained is that I know that I was really there. re-negotiating my relationship with technology and digital noise helped me feel more alive. like I am really here. my body is really here. it made me feel grounded to the place.

and it wasn't a place I was going to live in forever. it was very much about the present moment. but it gave me lessons as to how I want to be in relation to place, to myself, with my friend. it gave me a taste of what it feels like to be so fully there that I feel no grief for not being there anymore. and I still reference that period of time as a map of how I want to live no matter where I am.

the analogy that I think about is the difference between tasting food, but like really tasting food, like savoring food, versus getting all of your nutrition fed to you through a tube consumed in the form of, I don't know, soylent.

and I'm not saying that solving this digital distraction or digital noise problem will automatically make you the most present person, because there's infinite ways that we distract ourselves with our own minds. but it is just one way, one practice to consider.

slow acclimation through discovery

and I think that the process of acclimating, it takes time. and I'm not recommending anything drastic, unless drastic is what feels good and right for you. it takes a slow readjustment, the way you'd readjust to any new landscape or place that you arrive in.

I think what's most important in that transition is an attitude of discovery and curiosity. when there's less noise, what comes up? what is there for me to discover in relation to myself, in relation to the people that surround me, in relation to my community or this place I'm in?

because I'm not on Instagram or any platforms, people can't just send me a casual DM. they can't just comment on one of my newsletters. they have to write me an email and send it. and that takes effort, that takes accountability. the threshold for writing someone an email is much higher than liking something or even sharing something.

and so of course, when most of my digital life is just my website, my world, and my newsletter and this podcast, then the feedback I get is significantly reduced. but each missive that comes to me, each email that someone took the time to write and send me, it also creates a deeper ripple.

I receive them like pebbles. and when I turn my attention to them, I try to be as present as I can be, which means that maybe some emails won't get answered for a long time. I'm definitely guilty of that. but I'd rather savor the process of correspondence in a way that feels deliberate and slow, like snail mail, rather than be in a constant flurry of likes and retweets and repost and shares in a staticky digital world that ultimately doesn't feel very real.

valuing silence

and I think the point of all this is that you get to define what real means to you. you get to define what you value. and for me, I value the ability to be fully present with my creative practice, with my ideas, and with the people and places around me, reducing my intake of digital noise and knowing how to set boundaries around communication allows me to know which relationships and exchanges I want to give my energy to, not from a need of obligation or compulsion or anxiety, but because I choose to.

when you deliberately reduce the digital noise in your life, so many things come to the surface, both ideas, dreams, tugging, impulses, visions, and reoccurring fears and anxieties, part of it is trusting that the inner world can give you the direction and reoccurring impulses for you to tug on and explore. you can trust where your intuition leads you, where your curiosity guides you to.

and maybe the core question is, how can you practice valuing silence as much as our society values input, information, things to consume? how can valuing silence help you savor the ways in which you do exchange or be in conversation with others? it's kind of like valuing sleep as much as we value work or rest as much as we value productivity, or the yin as much as we value the yang, the act of surrender as much as we value going after what we want.

and of course, like many of my episodes, the whole point of this is that there is no real dichotomy. I think of silence as like a blanket of snow that cocoons and covers you and incubates you until the things beneath thaw and reveal itself.

and of course, it can be hard to be with all of the things underneath the silence, but I believe that those things are also portals deeper into yourself, that the way out the hard things is always through, which doesn't mean that you have to do it alone.

silence itself is not going to kill you. if anything, it will make you sharper, more attuned, more truly able to distinguish where you end and where others begin. maybe all of this is really a practice of boundaries, but more energetic information boundaries to treasure our awareness, our psyche, our consciousness as the most sacred spaces there are.

over time, what happens is that you stop hearing this static hum, the static-y-ness of constant noise and become more attuned to the native sounds of your inner landscapes.
